trial_name: PARAMEDIC2 — Epinephrine in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (2018)
citation: Perkins GD, Ji C, Deakin CD, et al. A randomized trial of epinephrine in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(8):711-721.
one_liner: Epinephrine increased 30-day survival but did not significantly improve neurologically favourable survival, with more severe disability among survivors.

pico.population: Adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by paramedics
pico.intervention: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes (max 10 doses)
pico.comparison: Placebo (0.9% saline) in identical syringes and schedule

background.existing_knowledge: Adrenaline has been embedded in adult ALS algorithms for decades for its α-adrenergic vasoconstrictor effect, but evidence for clinically meaningful outcomes was limited and conflicted.
background.knowledge_gap: Observational data were confounded by indication; it was unclear whether adrenaline improved long-term survival with good neurological function or merely increased ROSC at the cost of worse neurological outcomes.
background.hypothesis: Standard-dose epinephrine would improve 30-day survival compared with placebo, and any survival benefit would translate into more survivors with favourable neurological outcome (mRS 0–3).

methods.design: Pragmatic, individually randomised, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, prehospital trial with deferred consent.
methods.setting: Five UK NHS ambulance services (England and Wales); paramedic-led ALS; randomisation at the point a study drug pack was opened during ongoing resuscitation.

inclusion: Adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with resuscitation attempted by participating paramedics
Trial pack opened for IV/IO study-drug administration during ALS
exclusion: Arrest due to anaphylaxis or life-threatening asthma
Other protocol-specified ineligibility (e.g., DNAR status, ROSC before drug administration)

methods.intervention: Epinephrine 1 mg (10 mL of 1:10,000) IV or IO; non-shockable rhythms: as soon as IV/IO access achieved; shockable rhythms: after the third shock; repeated every 3–5 minutes, up to 10 doses.
methods.comparison: 0.9% saline in identical prefilled syringes, same dosing schedule and 10-dose cap.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (paramedics, receiving clinicians, outcome assessors, trial team); allocation concealed via identical packs/syringes.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 8000 to detect a 2% absolute difference in 30-day survival (6% vs 8%) with 93% power at two-sided 5% significance.
secondary_outcomes: Survival to discharge with favourable neurological outcome (mRS 0–3)
Survival at 3 months with favourable neurological outcome (mRS 0–3)
Severe neurological impairment among survivors at discharge (mRS 4–5)
methods.follow_up: Primary at 30 days; neurological outcomes at discharge and 3 months; longer-term follow-up at 6 and 12 months reported subsequently.

headline_bullets: Epinephrine increased 30-day survival from 2.4% to 3.2% (OR 1.39; 95% CI 1.06–1.82; P=0.02), NNT 112.
Large physiological signal: ROSC 36.3% vs 11.7%; sustained ROSC to hospital admission 23.8% vs 8.0% (OR 3.59).
No significant increase in favourable neurological survival at discharge (2.2% vs 1.9%) or 3 months (2.1% vs 1.6%).
Among survivors, severe disability at discharge (mRS 4–5) more frequent with epinephrine (31.0% vs 17.8%).

outcomes_table.outcome: Survival to discharge with favourable neurological outcome (mRS 0–3)
Survival at 3 months with favourable neurological outcome (mRS 0–3)
Severe neurological impairment among survivors at discharge (mRS 4–5)
outcomes_table.note: Reported among survivors; illustrates disability burden

outcomes_table.outcome: Median ICU length of stay among survivors (days)

safety: No specific safety concerns reported beyond the disability signal.

domains.notes: Individual allocation via concealed trial packs opened during resuscitation; 1:1 minimisation algorithm; allocation concealment robust due to indistinguishable packs/syringes.
Double-blind across prehospital and in-hospital phases; primary outcome objective; neurological outcome (mRS) more vulnerable but prespecified and standardised.
Modified ITT: 8103 packs opened, 87 excluded post-randomisation (plus 2 unknown allocation), leaving 8014 analysed; primary outcome ascertainment near-complete (99.9%).
Median call-to-drug time similar (21.5 vs 21.1 min); mean doses similar (4.9 vs 5.1); resuscitation duration modestly longer in epinephrine arm (47.5 vs 43.1 min).
Well balanced: age ~70 years, male ~65%, shockable rhythm ~19%, bystander CPR ~59%, medical cause ~91%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is strong overall (concealed allocation, double-blind, near-complete follow-up), modestly tempered by post-randomisation exclusions and modified ITT.

domains.notes: Typical adult OHCA case-mix (mean age ~70, ~78% non-shockable rhythms, ~59% bystander CPR); excludes children, pregnancy, anaphylaxis/asthma, and pre-EMS adrenaline.

Generalises well to paramedic-led ALS in high-income EMS systems with similar response intervals; not directly tested in physician-led systems with earlier drug delivery or in-hospital cardiac arrest; comparator was placebo, not alternative vasopressor.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is generally good for adult OHCA managed by paramedic-led ALS in high-income EMS systems, limited for excluded subgroups and settings with different prehospital care structure.

strengths: Large sample size (n=8014) with high event ascertainment for primary endpoint.
Rare prehospital placebo-controlled, double-blind design, directly addressing confounding by indication.
Pragmatic delivery embedded within routine ALS pathways across multiple ambulance services.
Clinically meaningful outcome hierarchy: 30-day survival plus functional neurological outcomes (mRS) at discharge and 3 months.
limitations: Modified ITT analysis and post-randomisation exclusions introduce small risk of bias vs strict ITT.
Absolute survival benefit small (0.8% at 30 days); estimates for favourable neurological survival imprecise due to low survivor numbers.
Median drug delivery time (~21 min from call) reflects real-world systems but limits inference about earlier administration.
mRS provides broad disability signal but may not capture cognitive and psychosocial morbidity typical after cardiac arrest.

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-conducted, pragmatic RCT that provides high-certainty evidence of a small survival benefit from epinephrine in OHCA, but no clear improvement in neurologically favourable survival, with a concerning increase in severe disability among survivors.
strengths: Near-complete follow-up for objective primary outcome
weaknesses: Limited generalisability to earlier drug delivery or in-hospital settings

sections.authors_conclusion: Epinephrine increased 30-day survival but did not significantly improve favourable neurological outcome, and increased severe neurological impairment among survivors.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Epinephrine remains a standard ALS drug for OHCA, but its benefit is primarily in achieving ROSC and hospital admission; the survival gain is small and comes with a trade-off of more severe disability among survivors.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult OHCA patients treated by paramedic-led ALS in systems with similar response intervals; most applicable to non-shockable rhythms.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Epinephrine should be withheld; it still improves survival, but clinicians and systems must weigh the survival–disability trade-off.
implementation_caveats: Guidelines continue to recommend epinephrine; timing and rhythm-based algorithms unchanged.
Shared decision-making and advance care planning may be informed by the quantified disability risk.
Systems should anticipate increased ICU/hospital utilisation from more ROSC and admissions.

controversies.notes: Absolute survival gain small (3.2% vs 2.4%), favourable neurological survival not significantly improved, and severe disability more common with epinephrine (31.0% vs 17.8%), challenging the ethical framing of 'benefit' in cardiac arrest trials.

At 6 months: favourable neurological outcome 2.0% vs 1.5% (adjusted OR 1.35; 95% CI 0.93–1.97); survival 2.9% vs 2.2% (adjusted OR 1.43; 95% CI 1.05–1.96). At 12 months: survival 2.7% vs 2.0% (adjusted OR 1.38; 95% CI 1.00–1.92). Functional, cognitive, and quality-of-life domains assessed but detailed differences not reported in abstract.
PARAMEDIC2 programme included an economic evaluation from NHS perspective (2016/17 GBP); cost-effectiveness results not reported in available abstract.
International guidelines (AHA 2025, ERC 2025) continue to incorporate epinephrine as standard therapy within adult ALS algorithms, with dosing and timing aligned to rhythm-based pathways.

context_related_trials.relation: Long-term outcomes of PARAMEDIC2 participants, reporting 6- and 12-month survival and neurological status.
Guideline update that incorporates PARAMEDIC2 evidence, continuing to recommend epinephrine in ALS.
European guideline update similarly maintaining epinephrine in ALS algorithms.

unresolved_questions: Would earlier epinephrine administration (e.g., first dose before 21 min) alter the survival–disability trade-off?
Is there a subgroup (e.g., initial shockable rhythm, witnessed arrest) that derives net benefit without increased disability?
Can post-resuscitation care be optimised to reduce severe neurological impairment in epinephrine-treated survivors?
What are the long-term functional, cognitive, and quality-of-life outcomes beyond mRS?

numbers_to_remember: Severe disability among survivors at discharge: 31.0% vs 17.8%
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Epinephrine increases ROSC and modestly improves survival but does not clearly improve neurologically favourable survival, and increases severe disability among survivors.
